claim: The amylase gene (AMY) underwent several gene copy number gains in humans.
source: The amylase gene (AMY), which codes for a starch-digesting enzyme in animals, underwent several gene copy number gains in humans (Perry et al., 2007), dogs (Axelsson et al., 2013), and mice (Schibler et al., 1982), possibly along with increased starch consumption during the evolution of these species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2007

claim: The amylase gene (AMY) underwent several gene copy number gains in dogs.
source: The amylase gene (AMY), which codes for a starch-digesting enzyme in animals, underwent several gene copy number gains in humans (Perry et al., 2007), dogs (Axelsson et al., 2013), and mice (Schibler et al., 1982), possibly along with increased starch consumption during the evolution of these species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2013

claim: The amylase gene (AMY) underwent several gene copy number gains in mice.
source: The amylase gene (AMY), which codes for a starch-digesting enzyme in animals, underwent several gene copy number gains in humans (Perry et al., 2007), dogs (Axelsson et al., 2013), and mice (Schibler et al., 1982), possibly along with increased starch consumption during the evolution of these species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schibler et al., 1982

claim: AMY gene copy number gains possibly occurred along with increased starch consumption during the evolution of humans, dogs, and mice.
source: The amylase gene (AMY), which codes for a starch-digesting enzyme in animals, underwent several gene copy number gains in humans (Perry et al., 2007), dogs (Axelsson et al., 2013), and mice (Schibler et al., 1982), possibly along with increased starch consumption during the evolution of these species.
evidence: Speculative statement about the relationship between copy number gains and starch consumption

claim: AMY copy number expansions independently occurred in several mammalian species which consume diets rich in starch.
source: Here, we present comprehensive evidence for AMY copy number expansions that independently occurred in several mammalian species which consume diets rich in starch.
evidence: Primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: AMY gene duplications may be an essential first step for amylase to be expressed in saliva.
source: We also provide correlative evidence that AMY gene duplications may be an essential first step for amylase to be expressed in saliva.
evidence: Correlative evidence from the study's data analysis

claim: Gene copy number amplification is a flexible and fast evolutionary mechanism that can independently occur in different branches of the phylogeny.
source: Our findings underscore the overall importance of gene copy number amplification as a flexible and fast evolutionary mechanism that can independently occur in different branches of the phylogeny.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings

claim: Diet has been a significant adaptive force in shaping human and nonhuman primate variation.
source: Diet has been a significant adaptive force in shaping human and nonhuman primate variation (Hardy et al., 2015; Milton, 1981; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The expansion of the copy number of the amylase gene occurred in concordance with the increase of starch consumption in the human lineage.
source: One of the best-described examples of diet-related adaptation is the expansion of the copy number of the amylase gene in concordance with the increase of starch consumption in the human lineage (Perry et al., 2007), likely postdating the human Neanderthal split (Inchley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2007

claim: The expansion of the copy number of the amylase gene in the human lineage likely postdated the human Neanderthal split.
source: One of the best-described examples of diet-related adaptation is the expansion of the copy number of the amylase gene in concordance with the increase of starch consumption in the human lineage (Perry et al., 2007), likely postdating the human Neanderthal split (Inchley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inchley et al., 2016

claim: A gene duplication in the ancestor of Old World monkeys and great apes led to the formation of two amylase genes (AMY2A and AMY2B) with pancreas-specific expression.
source: A gene duplication in the ancestor of Old World monkeys and great apes initially led to the formation of two amylase genes (AMY2A and AMY2B) with pancreas-specific expression (Samuelson et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samuelson et al., 1990

claim: A subsequent gene duplication in the ancestor of great apes led to the formation of AMY1 which gained salivary gland-specific expression.
source: Then, a subsequent gene duplication in the ancestor of great apes led to the formation of AMY1 which gained salivary gland-specific expression (Meisler and Ting, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meisler and Ting, 1993

claim: Further gene copy number gains of AMY1 in the human lineage led to increased expression of the AMY1 enzyme in human saliva.
source: In the human lineage, further gene copy number gains of AMY1 led to increased expression of the AMY1 enzyme in human saliva (Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2007

claim: Gene copy numbers of both AMY1 and AMY2 vary in different human populations.
source: Gene copy numbers of both AMY1 and AMY2 vary in different human populations (Carpenter et al., 2015; Usher et al., 2015), the former correlating with the extent of traditional starch consumption in these communities (Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carpenter et al., 2015 and Usher et al., 2015

claim: AMY1 copy number correlates with the extent of traditional starch consumption in different human populations.
source: Gene copy numbers of both AMY1 and AMY2 vary in different human populations (Carpenter et al., 2015; Usher et al., 2015), the former correlating with the extent of traditional starch consumption in these communities (Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2007

claim: Mice, rats, and pigs express substantial levels of amylase in their saliva.
source: For example, it was shown that mice, rats, and pigs express substantial levels of amylase in their saliva (Boehlke et al., 2015; Janiak, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Boehlke et al., 2015 and Janiak, 2016

claim: The amylase locus has been shown to be evolving under positive selection in dogs and in house mice.
source: In addition, the amylase locus has been shown to be evolving under positive selection in dogs and in house mice (Reiter et al., 2016; Staubach et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reiter et al., 2016 and Staubach et al., 2012

claim: Dogs gained multiple copies of the amylase gene after their split from the wolf 30,000–40,000 years ago.
source: Recent studies, for instance, have shown that dogs gained multiple copies of the amylase gene after their split from the wolf 30,000–40,000 years ago (Skoglund et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skoglund et al., 2015

claim: Dogs gaining multiple copies of the amylase gene might likely be a result of their domestication, which exposed them to human food leftovers rich in starch.
source: This might likely be a result of their domestication, which exposed them to human food leftovers rich in starch (Axelsson et al., 2013; Botigué et al., 2017; Ollivier et al., 2016; Reiter et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by multiple citations

claim: Some Old World monkeys have substantial amylase enzymatic activity in their saliva, despite missing the amylase duplication found in great apes.
source: For instance, it is not known why some Old World monkeys have substantial amylase enzymatic activity in their saliva, despite missing the amylase duplication found in great apes (Janiak, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janiak, 2016

claim: Humans can have up to five more haploid copies of the amylase gene than chimpanzees.
source: Up to five more haploid copies of the amylase gene can be found in humans than in chimpanzees.
evidence: Statement of known fact from prior research

claim: Copy number variation of amylase was noted in pigs.
source: Copy number variation was also noted in pigs (Paudel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paudel et al., 2013

claim: The study conducted a digital droplet polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR)-based analysis of amylase gene copy numbers from 204 DNA samples across 46 species.
source: To comprehensively investigate amylase gene copy number gains in other mammalian lineages, we conducted a digital droplet polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR)-based analysis of amylase gene copy numbers from 204 DNA samples across 46 species encompassing all major branches of the mammalian phylogeny.
evidence: Description of experimental methods used in the study

claim: Bursts of amylase gene copy number were discovered in mice, rats, pigs, and boars in addition to humans and dogs.
source: In addition to humans and dogs, we discovered similar bursts (i.e. gains of more than one copy) of amylase gene copy number in mice, rats, pigs, and boars (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Primary finding from the study's ddPCR analysis, referenced in figures

claim: Amylase genes within a given species are more similar to each other than they are to those of other species.
source: Our results showed that amylase genes within a given species are more similar to each other than they are to those of other species.
evidence: Result from phylogenetic analysis conducted in the study

claim: Duplications of the amylase gene might have occurred in each lineage independently.
source: One explanation for this observation could be that duplications of the amylase gene might have occurred in each lineage independently.

claim: A retrotransposon (HERV_a_int) was inserted upstream of a new amylase gene duplicate (AMY1) in the ancestor of great apes.
source: They identified a retrotransposon (HERV_a_int) inserted upstream of a new amylase gene duplicate (AMY1) in the ancestor of great apes (Samuelson et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samuelson et al., 1990

claim: The HERV_a_int retrotransposon was found to be associated with all the additional AMY1 copies detected in humans.
source: This retrotransposon was found to be associated with all the additional AMY1 copies detected in humans (Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2007

claim: The duplications of AMY1 occurred after the human-chimpanzee phylogenetic split.
source: This finding strongly supported the notion that the duplications of AMY1 occurred after the human-chimpanzee phylogenetic split (Perry et al., 2007; Samuelson et al., 1990).

claim: A mouse lineage-specific retrotransposon (L1Md_T) was found in the upstream region of five out of the seven mouse amylase gene copies.
source: Indeed, we found a mouse lineage-specific retrotransposon (L1Md_T) in the upstream region of five out of the seven mouse amylase gene copies.

claim: By ddPCR analysis, 9–13 diploid copies of the amylase gene were found in brown rats and 6–7 copies in black rats and wood rats.
source: By ddPCR analysis, we found 9–13 diploid copies of the amylase gene in brown rats and 6–7 copies in black rats and wood rats (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Result from ddPCR experimental analysis

claim: The L1Md_T retrotransposon was not found in rats.
source: However, the L1Md_T retrotransposon was not found in rats.

claim: A rat-specific retrotransposon (L1_Rat3) was found inserted upstream of two out of the three rat amylase copies in the assembled rat reference genome.
source: When we investigated the amylase locus in the rat genome, we found a rat-specific retrotransposon (L1_Rat3) inserted upstream of two out of the three rat amylase copies in the assembled rat reference genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Result from genomic analysis of rat reference genome, shown in Figure 2B

claim: Amylase gene duplications in rats likely occurred independently from the ones in mice.
source: Therefore, amylase gene duplications in rats likely occurred independently from the ones in mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from retrotransposon analysis

claim: A canid-specific L1 element (L1_Canid) was found in all four amylase gene copies assembled across three different contigs in dogs.
source: In dogs, we found a canid-specific L1 element (L1_Canid) in all four amylase gene copies assembled across three different contigs.
evidence: Result from genomic analysis of dog reference genome

claim: An older lineage-specific L1 element (L1M3) was found downstream of all six amylase copies assembled across three contigs in pigs.
source: In pigs, we found an older lineage-specific L1 element (L1M3) downstream of all six amylase copies assembled across three contigs.
evidence: Result from genomic analysis of pig reference genome

claim: Lineage-specific retrotransposons were found located in similar proximity (0.8–4.2 kb upstream or downstream) to multiple amylase gene copies in human, mouse, rat, pig, and dog reference genomes.
source: Overall, we found lineage-specific retrotransposons located in similar proximity (0.8–4.2 kb upstream or downstream) to multiple amylase gene copies in human, mouse, rat, pig, and dog reference genomes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Summary of genomic analysis results shown in Figure 2B

claim: The respective retrotransposons are in identical positions relative to the amylase gene within each species.
source: In each of these cases, the respective retrotransposons are in identical positions relative to the amylase gene within each species.
evidence: Result from comparative genomic analysis

claim: These retrotransposons inserted in proximity to an ancestral amylase copy in each species independently and were subsequently duplicated along with further gained amylase gene copies.
source: We surmised that these retrotransposons inserted in proximity to an ancestral amylase copy in each species independently and were subsequently duplicated along with further gained amylase gene copies.
evidence: Inference drawn from retrotransposon analysis

claim: Lineage-specific retrotransposons accompanying amylase gene copy number gains in humans, mice, rats, dogs, and pigs clearly point to lineage-specific duplications as a major driver of amylase gene copy number bursts in these species.
source: However, the fact that lineage-specific retrotransposons accompany amylase gene copy number gains in humans, mice, rats, dogs, and pigs, clearly points to lineage-specific duplications as a major driver of amylase gene copy number bursts in these species.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from retrotransposon analysis

claim: Ancestrally, amylase was a pancreatic enzyme in mammals.
source: Ancestrally, amylase was a pancreatic enzyme in mammals.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: In certain mammalian species, amylase became expressed also in saliva.
source: However, in certain mammalian species, amylase became expressed also in saliva (Chauncey et al., 1963).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chauncey et al., 1963

claim: The retrotransposon insertion along with the AMY1 duplicate in the ancestor of great apes was responsible for tissue-specific expression of this gene in salivary glands.

claim: Previous studies hypothesized that a similar, but independent gene duplication event led to the expression of amylase also in the saliva of mice.
source: Previous studies hypothesized that a similar, but independent gene duplication event led to the expression of amylase also in the saliva of mice (Meisler and Ting, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meisler and Ting, 1993

claim: In most mammals starch digestion primarily occurs through the activity of the pancreatic enzyme in the intestines rather than in the mouth.
source: Even though amylase is a digestive enzyme, it is clear that in most mammals starch digestion primarily occurs through the activity of the pancreatic enzyme in the intestines rather than in the mouth (Fernández and Wiley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernández and Wiley, 2017

claim: The study provides the most comprehensive documentation of salivary amylase activity in mammals, encompassing 127 saliva samples across 22 species.
source: Currently, our study provides the most comprehensive documentation of salivary amylase activity in mammals, encompassing 127 saliva samples across 22 species (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Salivary amylase activity was observed in some New World monkeys, boars, dogs, deer mice, woodrats, and giant African pouched rats.
source: In addition to species that were already known to express amylase in their saliva, we observed salivary amylase activity in some New World monkeys, boars, dogs, deer mice, woodrats, and giant African pouched rats (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Amylase activity in dog saliva varies from breed to breed.
source: It is important to note here that our findings also suggest that amylase activity in dog saliva varies from breed to breed (Supplementary file 1).

claim: The copy annotated as mouse amy1 is expressed in salivary glands, while the other amylase gene duplicates have a negligible expression in that tissue.

evidence: Result from RNA-Seq data analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Mouse amy1 is not orthologous to human AMY1.
source: However, mouse amy1 is not orthologous to human AMY1 (Meisler and Ting, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meisler and Ting, 1993

claim: The amino acid sequence of mouse amy1 is distinct from those of other amylase copies in the mouse genome.
source: Furthermore, its amino acid sequence is distinct from those of other amylase copies in the mouse genome.
evidence: Result from sequence analysis

claim: The distinct amy1 sequence is shared with rat and other rodents including deer mouse, vole, Mongolian gerbil, and golden hamster.
source: This distinct amy1 sequence is shared with rat and other rodents including deer mouse, vole, Mongolian gerbil, and golden hamster.

claim: The duplication event that led to the formation of mouse amy1 likely occurred in an ancestor of muroidea.

claim: The more recently acquired, mouse and rat-specific amylase gene duplications are not expressed in mouse salivary glands.
source: Interestingly, the more recently acquired, mouse and rat-specific amylase gene duplications are not expressed in mouse salivary glands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: No mammalian species that underwent a 'burst' of amylase gene copy number was found without concurrent salivary amylase activity.
source: We could not find a mammalian species that underwent a 'burst' of amylase gene copy number that did not show concurrent salivary amylase activity (Figure 3C).

claim: No species with less than four diploid amylase copies showed any measurable amylase activity in saliva.
source: Also, we found no species with less than four diploid amylase copies that showed any measurable amylase activity in saliva.
evidence: Result from comparative analysis of copy number and salivary activity data

claim: The relationship between amylase gene copy number and salivary amylase activity cannot be explained by linear correlation.
source: It is important to note here that the relationship between amylase gene copy number and salivary amylase activity cannot be explained by linear correlation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data analysis

claim: Rhesus macaques and baboons have relatively low amylase gene copy numbers (5–6 diploid copies) but show high amylase activity in their saliva (514–1,652 units per mg of total protein).
source: For example, rhesus macaques and baboons have relatively low amylase gene copy numbers (5–6 diploid copies) but show high amylase activity in their saliva (514–1,652 units per mg of total protein).

claim: Dogs showed some of the highest gene copy numbers of amylase among mammals (9–19 diploid copies) but express very low amounts of amylase in their saliva (0–9 units/mg).
source: In contrast, dogs, which among mammals showed some of the highest gene copy numbers of amylase (9–19 diploid copies), express very low amounts of amylase in their saliva (0–9 units/mg).

claim: A gene duplication may be a necessary condition for amylase to become expressed in saliva.
source: Overall, these results suggest that a gene duplication may be a necessary condition for amylase to become expressed in saliva.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis of copy number and expression data

claim: Different regulatory architectures are likely responsible for the differences in amylase activity observed in saliva across different mammalian species.
source: Subsequently, however, different regulatory architectures are likely responsible for the differences in amylase activity observed in saliva across different mammalian species.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that copy number does not linearly correlate with expression

claim: In humans, it has been postulated that starch consumption has driven the increased gene copy number of the amylase gene through positive selection.
source: For humans, it has been postulated that starch consumption has driven the increased gene copy number of the amylase gene through positive selection (Perry et al., 2007).

claim: For dogs, the rapid amylase gene copy number increase as compared to wolves (3–8 haploid copy number gain) has been associated with a transition during their domestication from a primarily meat-based diet to a diet enriched in starch.
source: For dogs, the rapid amylase gene copy number increase as compared to wolves (3–8 haploid copy number gain) has been associated with a transition during their domestication from a primarily meat-based diet to a diet enriched in starch (Axelsson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2013

claim: Species consuming a broad-range diet generally harbor significantly higher copy numbers of the amylase gene.
source: We found that species consuming a broad-range diet generally harbor significantly higher copy numbers of the amylase gene (Figure 4A).

claim: The mean diploid amylase copy number among animals consuming specialized diets is 2.4, while it is 7.0 for those consuming broad-range diets.
source: Specifically, the mean diploid amylase copy number among animals consuming specialized diets is 2.4, while it is 7.0 for those consuming broad-range diets.

claim: Corrected for phylogenetic dependence, a broad-range diet is significantly associated with increased amylase gene copy number (p =~9×10−6).
source: Corrected for phylogenetic dependence, a broad-range diet is significantly associated with increased amylase gene copy number (p =~9×10−6).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis correcting for phylogenetic relationships

claim: Species that over recent evolutionary time gained access to abundant starch-rich foods harbor considerably higher copy numbers of the amylase gene.
source: Among species that consume a broad-range diet, we found that those who over recent evolutionary time gained access to abundant starch-rich foods — either through domestication (as in the case of dogs and pigs) or through dietary commensalism with humans (as in the case of house mice or brown and black rats) — harbor considerably higher copy numbers of the amylase gene (Figure 4A).

claim: The mean diploid amylase gene copy number is 11.6 for species consuming a starch-rich diet, while it is 5.0 for those that consume lower amounts of starch in their diet.
source: The mean diploid amylase gene copy number is 11.6 for species consuming a starch-rich diet, while it is 5.0 for those that consume lower amounts of starch in their diet.
evidence: Statistical summary of copy number data

claim: When corrected for phylogenetic dependence, starch consumption (categorized into high- and low-starch content in diet) is significantly correlated with amylase gene copy number (p =~10−4).
source: When corrected for phylogenetic dependence, starch consumption (categorized into high- and low-starch content in diet) is significantly correlated with amylase gene copy number (p =~10−4).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis correcting for phylogenetic relationships

claim: Mammals consuming a broad-range diet express on average a thousand-fold higher amylase activity in their saliva (~243.6 units/mg of total salivary protein) than those consuming specialized diets (~0.1 units/mg).
source: We found that mammals consuming a broad-range diet also express on average a thousand-fold higher amylase activity in their saliva (~243.6 units/mg of total salivary protein) than those consuming specialized diets (~0.1 units/mg) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Result from comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: When corrected for phylogenetic dependence, consumption of a broad-range diet is significantly associated with the enzymatic activity of amylase in saliva (p =~10−4).
source: When corrected for phylogenetic dependence, it appeared that consumption of a broad-range diet is significantly associated with the enzymatic activity of amylase in saliva (p =~10−4).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis correcting for phylogenetic relationships

claim: Salivary expression of amylase is not associated with the amount of starch consumption per se.
source: Salivary expression of amylase, however, turned out to not be associated with the amount of starch consumption per se (Figure 4B).
evidence: Result from comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Salivary expression of amylase appeared to be associated with the consumption of starch, regardless of the amount.
source: Rather, salivary expression of amylase appeared to be associated with the consumption of starch, regardless of the amount.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis

claim: Previous work in humans and in rats showed that salivary amylase is linked to the perception of starch.
source: Previous work in humans and in rats showed that salivary amylase is linked to the perception of starch (Mandel et al., 2010; Sclafani et al., 1987).

claim: The ability to enzymatically liberate sugar from long-chain starch molecules for the perception of sweet taste might have provided a metabolic fitness advantage to mammalian species consuming a broad range diet.

claim: Lemurs express negligible amylase activity in their saliva (~0.009 units/mg).

claim: For marmosets and lemurs, starch is not a primary component in their otherwise diverse diet.

claim: Lemurs consume tamarind fruit, reportedly rich in non-starch polysaccharides.

claim: In dogs, an increase was found not only in amylase gene copy number but also in enzymatic activity of amylase in saliva as compared to the carnivorous wolf.

claim: Dogs diverged from wolves approximately 30,000–40,000 years ago.

claim: No difference of amylase gene copy numbers and salivary enzymatic activity was found between domesticated pigs and wild boars.

claim: The results suggest yet another occurrence of gene copy number gain in the ancestor of New World monkeys.
source: Assuming that the ancestral state of this lineage had one haploid copy, our results suggest yet another occurrence of gene copy number gain in the ancestor of New World monkeys.

claim: An additional amylase gene copy was found in capuchins, which generally consume more starch than other New World monkeys.
source: Moreover, we found an additional amylase gene copy in capuchins, which generally consume more starch than other New World monkeys (Galetti and Pedroni, 1994; Rowe and Myers, 2016).
evidence: Result from copy number analysis, supported by citations about diet

claim: Lemurs harbor only one haploid copy of the amylase gene.
source: Next, we investigated lemurs, an outgroup primate species to monkeys and great apes, and found that they indeed only harbor one haploid copy of the amylase gene (Figure 5).
evidence: Result from copy number analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The result in the lemur lineage, combined with prior reports that ancestors of simians have a single amylase gene copy, suggests that primate ancestors possessed only one haploid copy of the amylase gene.
source: Our result in the lemur lineage, combined with prior reports that ancestors of simians have a single amylase gene copy (Samuelson et al., 1996; Samuelson et al., 1990), suggests that primate ancestors possessed only one haploid copy of the amylase gene.
evidence: Inference drawn from current data and prior reports

claim: Several species of Old World monkeys, including rhesus macaques and baboons, express high enzymatic activity of amylase in their saliva.
source: We found that several species of Old World monkeys, including rhesus macaques and baboons, express high enzymatic activity of amylase in their saliva (Figure 5) (Mau et al., 2010).
evidence: Result from salivary activity measurements shown in Figure 5, supported by citation

claim: Primates belonging to the subfamily cercopithecinae are known for their cheek pouches in which they store food for prolonged oral predigestion.

claim: The primate subfamily cercopithecinae could be an exception in that salivary amylase may substantially participate in oral digestion of starch.
source: Thus, this primate subfamily could be an exception in that salivary amylase may substantially participate in oral digestion of starch.

claim: Most New World monkeys do not consume starch in their regular diets.

claim: Marmosets primarily consume insects and plant exudate.

claim: Owl monkeys consume flowers, insects, nectar, and leaves.

claim: The results in primates document two additional instances (cercopithecinae and capuchins) where duplications of the amylase gene coincide with salivary expression.
source: Our results in primates document two additional instances (cercopithecinae and capuchins) where duplications of the amylase gene coincide with salivary expression.
evidence: Summary of findings from primate analysis

claim: The evolution of the amylase locus in primates followed the same general trends observed for all mammals in that dietary strategies coincide both with amylase gene copy number and salivary expression in a lineage-specific manner.
source: Combined, our results suggest that the evolution of the amylase locus in primates followed the same general trends observed for all mammals in that dietary strategies coincide both with amylase gene copy number and salivary expression in a lineage-specific manner.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis across primates and other mammals

claim: Multiple bursts of amylase copy number gains occurred independently in different branches of the mammalian phylogeny.
source: Our results reveal a staggering diversity of amylase gene copy numbers across extant mammals that consume starch. We report multiple bursts of amylase copy number gains that occurred independently in different branches of the mammalian phylogeny.
evidence: Summary of primary findings

claim: Each burst of amylase copy number gains coincided with expression of amylase in saliva.
source: Our results showed that each of these bursts coincided with expression of amylase in saliva.
evidence: Summary of primary findings

claim: Phylogenetically distant species living in different habitats and consuming different diets have arrived at astonishingly similar amylase gene copy numbers, which correlate with the level of starch in their diet.
source: Our results also showed that phylogenetically distant species living in different habitats and consuming different diets have arrived at astonishingly similar amylase gene copy numbers, which correlate with the level of starch in their diet.
evidence: Summary of primary findings

claim: The amylase locus evolved under the influence of the dietary context driven by the functional importance of amylase enzymatic activity in two digestive gland systems, namely the salivary glands and the pancreas.
source: We posit here that the amylase locus evolved under the influence of the dietary context driven by the functional importance of amylase enzymatic activity in two digestive gland systems, namely the salivary glands, located at the entrance to the gastrointestinal tract, and the pancreas located further distally in the digestive continuum.
evidence: Proposed model based on study findings

claim: Increase in gene copy number leads to higher amylase expression in the pancreas, which in turn allows rapid and effective intestinal digestion of starch in species consuming a higher amount of that food component in their diet.
source: It has been suggested that increase in gene copy number leads to higher amylase expression in the pancreas, which in turn allows rapid and effective intestinal digestion of starch in species consuming a higher amount of that food component in their diet (Axelsson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2013

claim: At least one gene duplication is required for amylase to gain expression in salivary glands.
source: Based on our findings, we propose here that at least one gene duplication is required for amylase to gain expression in salivary glands.
evidence: Proposed model based on study findings

claim: The gain of salivary gland expression is a form of neofunctionalization where an otherwise intact gene copy acquires mutations in its regulatory architecture, thus leading to expression in a new tissue.
source: We argue that this is a form of neofunctionalization (Ohno S, 1970) where an otherwise intact gene copy acquires mutations in its regulatory architecture, thus leading to expression in a new tissue, in this case the salivary gland system.
evidence: Proposed model based on study findings, with citation to Ohno S, 1970

claim: One or more gene duplication events of the salivary-specific copy are needed to gain a level of enzymatic activity in saliva optimally suited to accommodate starch predigestion in the mouth environment.
source: We hypothesize that one or more gene duplication events of this copy are needed to gain a level of enzymatic activity in saliva optimally suited to accommodate starch predigestion in the mouth environment.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on study findings

claim: Muroidea and cercopithecinae possess only a single salivary-gland-specific gene copy but arrive at high levels of amylase activity in their saliva.

claim: A strong regulatory element is associated with the single salivary-gland-specific copy in muroidea and cercopithecinae.
source: In this case, we surmise that a strong regulatory element is associated with that single copy.

claim: In addition to the salivary-specific copy, muroidea possess multiple other amylase gene copies that are not expressed in salivary gland tissue.
source: In addition to that copy, muroidea possess multiple other amylase gene copies that are not expressed in salivary gland tissue.
evidence: Result from expression analysis

claim: Dogs and pigs have numbers of amylase gene copies comparable to humans and some muroidea but show much less amylase activity in their saliva than these species.
source: Dogs and pigs have numbers of amylase gene copies comparable to humans and some muroidea but show much less amylase activity in their saliva than these species.
evidence: Result from comparative analysis of copy number and expression

claim: In humans, the number of amylase gene copy numbers was shown to correlate with levels of amylase expression in saliva.
source: In humans, the number of amylase gene copy numbers was shown to correlate with levels of amylase expression in saliva (Bank et al., 1992; Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bank et al., 1992 and Perry et al., 2007

claim: Across all mammalian species, a simple correlation between copy number and salivary expression does not hold true.
source: Our data show that across all mammalian species such a simple correlation does not hold true.
evidence: Result from comparative analysis across species

claim: A correlation of amylase gene copy number and salivary enzyme activity was shown for dog (R2 = 0.45) and pig (R2 = 0.69).
source: In this regard, we could show a correlation of amylase gene copy number and salivary enzyme activity for dog (R2 = 0.45) and pig (R2 = 0.69).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis within species

claim: Amylase gene copy numbers generally correlate with a broad-range diet and with high versus low-starch consumption.
source: From a broader ecological perspective, we showed that amylase gene copy numbers generally correlate with a broad-range diet and with high versus low-starch consumption.
evidence: Summary of ecological findings

claim: Salivary amylase activity is only correlated with broad-range diet but not with the amount of starch.
source: However, salivary amylase activity is only correlated with broad-range diet but not with the amount of starch.
evidence: Summary of ecological findings

claim: Most mammalian species do not keep food long enough in their mouth for salivary amylase to substantially participate in starch digestion.
source: As a matter of fact, most mammalian species do not keep food long enough in their mouth for salivary amylase to substantially participate in starch digestion.
evidence: Statement based on general knowledge of mammalian feeding behavior

claim: In most mammalian species the role of amylase in saliva may be to liberate oligomeric sugar molecules from polymeric starch chains that can then be perceived by sweet-taste receptors in the oral cavity.
source: We argue here that in most mammalian species the role of amylase in saliva may be to liberate oligomeric sugar molecules from polymeric starch chains that can then be perceived by sweet-taste receptors in the oral cavity.
evidence: Proposed functional explanation based on prior research

claim: Studies found links between salivary amylase and taste perception.
source: Indeed, studies found links between salivary amylase and taste perception (Mandel et al., 2010; Sclafani et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mandel et al., 2010 and Sclafani et al., 1987

claim: Being able to perceive otherwise tasteless starch in their diet might confer an adaptive advantage to species consuming broad-range diets by enabling them to detect high caloric (i.e. starch-containing), food components.
source: Being able to perceive otherwise tasteless starch in their diet might confer an adaptive advantage to species consuming broad-range diets by enabling them to detect high caloric (i.e. starch-containing), food components.
evidence: Speculative evolutionary explanation

claim: In cheek-pouched cercopithecinae, which conduct almost half of their starch digestion in the oral cavity, salivary amylase may have evolved to substantially participate in the overall digestion of dietary starch.
source: An exceptional example are the cheek-pouched cercopithecinae where putative fitness advantage of salivary amylase expression goes beyond taste perception. In these species, which conduct almost half of their starch digestion in the oral cavity (Janiak, 2016), salivary amylase may have evolved to substantially participate in the overall digestion of dietary starch, a role executed by pancreatic amylase in most other species.
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to Janiak, 2016

claim: Salivary amylase may be involved in the regulation of metabolic glucose homeostasis.
source: In addition to gustatory and digestive functions, salivary amylase may also be involved in the regulation of metabolic glucose homeostasis (Peyrot des Gachons and Breslin, 2016) as well as associated with bacterial composition in the oral cavity (Davenport, 2017; Scannapieco et al., 1989) or in the gut (Poole et al., 2019).

claim: Salivary amylase may be associated with bacterial composition in the oral cavity.
source: In addition to gustatory and digestive functions, salivary amylase may also be involved in the regulation of metabolic glucose homeostasis (Peyrot des Gachons and Breslin, 2016) as well as associated with bacterial composition in the oral cavity (Davenport, 2017; Scannapieco et al., 1989) or in the gut (Poole et al., 2019).
